svg.title: Fifteen counter-intuitive truths about multicast design, each with the mechanism and the number behind it
svg.desc: A three by five grid of cards. Each card states one truth: reverse check of the source, a broadcast domain problem, the RP as a single point, SPT switchover is not free, SSM as the modern default, no retransmission, scarce addresses, control and data plane decoupled, unidirectional trees, four different roles, bandwidth multiplication, silent failures, state count as the bottleneck, playing versus playing the right path, and rate limiting plus boundaries as the last defence. A bottom band notes that each truth is a line item in the design document.
svg.text: Fifteen truths, fifteen design checks
If a design document answers all fifteen, multicast will not surprise you in acceptance
No destination lookup, only source check
Ingress interface must equal the path to the
source. 90% of "no video" dies at show ip rpf.
It is a broadcast domain problem
Without snooping a 5 Mbps stream x 500 access
ports = 2.5 Gbps of traffic nobody asked for.
The RP is a single point plus state centre
Established (S,G) keep forwarding when it dies,
but no new join and no new register succeeds.
SPT switchover is not free
Default behaviour: one (S,G) per receiver branch
on the source side. spt-threshold infinity is a lever.
SSM is the modern default answer
All the complexity comes from not knowing the
source. 232/8 + IGMPv3 removes the RP entirely.
No retransmission, no congestion control
A lost packet is lost for good. It relies on a
congestion-free path, a stable tree, a clean L2.
Addresses are a scarce resource
32 IP groups collapse onto 1 MAC. Plan 239/8
like 10/8: site block, service block, index.
Control plane and data plane are independent
A correct mroute proves nothing about the hardware:
replication resources, TCAM, unprogrammed line cards.
Multicast is unidirectional
Only a receiver join builds tree state. The source
cannot create a tree, and cannot tear one down.
Four roles, four different meanings
Querier (lowest IP), DR (highest priority/IP),
Assert winner (per S,G), DF (per group, toward RP).
Bandwidth is not the stream bandwidth
Stream x branches x (1 + redundancy). Layer 2 does
not amplify in L3 but does per port: 8 x 24 = 192 Mbps.
Failures are silent
No ICMP, no syslog, no retransmission. Only active
observation at five layers finds them.
State count, not bandwidth, is the bottleneck
SM = (*,G) + (S,G); SSM = (S,G); BiDir = (*,G).
32K entries against an 80K requirement fails.
"It plays" is not "it plays the right path"
A wrong tree still delivers pixels, 20 ms late and
one fibre short. Acceptance must test the shape.
Rate limiting and boundaries, not trust
One 1 Mbps source can fill 100 gigabit links.
Every boundary needs a rate and a scope.
Read the list as a checklist, not as theory
Each truth has an addressable artefact: an RPF table, a snooping baseline, an RP redundancy plan, a state budget, a rate limit, an acceptance test.
